newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria chancellor says coalition not in danger.
newsitem.headline: Austria chancellor says coalition not in danger.

text.p: Austria's Social Democrat Chancellor Franz Vranitzky on Friday dismissed suggestions his one-year-old government was in danger of collapsing over the imminent privatisation of the country's second biggest bank.

But tension remained high within his coalition with the conservative People's Party, who oppose the likely sell-off of Creditanstalt-Bankverein to a rival bank indirectly controlled by the Social Democrats.
Vranitzky, Europe's longest-serving government leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said he was convinced the coalition would survive.
"Nobody, including the (People's Party) is seriously questioning the coalition," he told Austrian radio.
But the chancellor expressed the same optimism during bitter budget talks in October 1995, when a coalition of the same two parties crumbled, leading to a snap election in December that year.

The Social Democrats and the conservatives, led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, managed to agree on one thing on Thursday -- to bring forward an emergency meeting of coalition leaders on the privatisation from Monday to Saturday afternoon.
The meeting will be attended by Vranitzky, Schuessel, Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima, conservative Economics Minister Johann Farnleitner and both party whips.

Far-right leader Joerg Haider, eager to exploit the government split, said on Thursday his Freedom Party had already had a series of talks with the People's Party on the bank sale ahead of a special parliament session next Tuesday.

Together the People's Party and the far right could command a majority in parliament and, if pushed, Schuessel could try to embarrass Vranitzky by outvoting the Social Democrats -- a move which could harm the coalition beyond repair.
Senior Social Democrats said on Friday they would demand an explanation from the conservatives about their talks with the far right at Saturday's emergency coalition meeting.
The Creditanstalt sell-off, seven years in the making, has developed into more than just a straight privatisation.
The bank sale has exposed a serious behind-the-scenes power struggle between the two big parties which have ruled Austria alone or together since the end of World War Two.

Creditanstalt, bankers to the Habsburg emperors during its 141-year history, is still regarded as a conservative fiefdom. The party wants Creditanstalt to be sold to an international consortium led by Italian-controlled insurer EA-Generali.
A takeover by Bank Austria, which banking sources say is more or less on the cards, would do more than rankle Schuessel's People's Party.

Bank Austria is effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna and its acquisition of Creditanstalt would mark a symbolic blow to the conservatives, who fear Vranitzky's party is trying to consolidate its hold of Austria's overcrowded banking industry.
Creditanstalt's nearly 8,000 employees, many of whom are likely to be conservative voters, fear big job losses if Bank Austria takes over the bank.

The deadline for last bids for the bank expired on Friday morning and Klima said he would probably make a decision before Tuesday. That will also anger the conservatives who have advised Klima to hold his fire until after parliament meets.
